notes.Agate Assault: 4 damage, or artifact removal when you need it.
notes.Banishing Light: Exiles anything. Slightly below average by GIH, still a top removal pick.

notes.Carrot Cake: Two bodies, two scrys and a Food. The best white common.
notes.Dire Downdraft: Blue's best common. Tucks a creature and gets cheap against attackers.
notes.Downwind Ambusher: Flash. Finishes off a damaged creature or shrinks one.
notes.Galewind Moose: Flash, vigilance, reach and trample on a big body.
notes.Glidedive Duo: A flyer that drains 2. WB and BR both want it.
notes.Harvestrite Host: Rabbit engine that pumps and draws as rabbits enter.
notes.Heartfire Hero: The valiant payoff. Grows with every target and burns the opponent when it dies.
notes.Hop to It: Three bodies for 3 mana. Tokens for GW and other wide decks.
notes.Hunter's Talent: Removal plus a lasting attack bonus.
notes.Intrepid Rabbit: A 3-drop with a combat trick attached, plus offspring for value.
notes.Overprotect: Wins a combat or saves a creature from removal.
notes.Pearl of Wisdom: Draw two, cheaper with an otter. Often wheels.
notes.Polliwallop: Bite at instant speed, cheaper with frogs.
notes.Savor: The best common in the set. Kills X/2s and leaves a Food behind.
notes.Scales of Shale: Underrated trick. Lifelink and indestructible, cheap with lizards.
notes.Shoreline Looter: Blue's best uncommon. Card advantage that can't be blocked.

notes.Splash Lasher: Stuns on entry, and offspring adds a second stun.
notes.Sugar Coat: Turns a creature into a Food. Close enough to removal.
notes.Take Out the Trash: 3 damage at instant speed. Red's best common.

notes.Treeguard Duo: Turns a wide board into a big alpha strike.
notes.Wick's Patrol: Removal stapled to a 6-drop that mills itself toward threshold.

text: Rabbits, bats, birds and mice. The best common removal and wide boards; good in every pair. Draftsim ranks it second and the data agree it is one of the three deep colours.

Birds, frogs, otters and rats. Tempo, flyers and card draw, but no common hard removal. The weakest commons in the set (none reaches 57) with decent uncommons. Underdrafted, so its commons wheel and the colour is often open. Draftsim ranks it last.
Bats, lizards, rats and squirrels. The deepest uncommons in the set and the best cheap removal. Draftsim ranks it third; by win rate its uncommons are ahead of every other colour's.
Mice, lizards, otters and raccoons. Aggressive, with burn for removal. The weakest colour in the set at both common and uncommon. Draftsim puts it fourth, and its mythic Season is the one to pass.
Frogs, rabbits, raccoons and squirrels. Fight spells and big bodies, the best commons of any colour, and the only colour that splashes comfortably. Draftsim ranks it first.

archetypes.name: Flying midrange

text: Flying midrange that buffs the ground team whenever flyers enter. One of the two weakest pairs; blue's thin commons hold it back.

sections.heading: Tribes in winning decks
text: Winning WU decks run about 6 Birds cards among their 23 spells. The second tribe is usually Rabbits.

key: Buffs your ground creatures when flyers enter.
A bird payoff people rate higher than its win rate.

archetypes.name: Threshold control

text: Self-mill, surveil and loot until seven cards are in your graveyard, then the payoffs switch on. Slow to get going and strong late. It is the one archetype whose package showed a clear effect on deck win rate.

sections.heading: Tribes in winning decks
text: Winning UB decks run about 7 Rats cards among their 23 spells. The second tribe is usually Squirrels, Otters or Frogs.

key: Menace and a bounce once threshold is on.
Makes rats every turn creatures die.

archetypes.name: Life-loss aggro

text: Make the opponent lose life early with pingers, menace and drain, then cast payoffs that check whether they lost life this turn. The best deck in the format by win rate. Black supplies the removal and red the reach.

sections.heading: Tribes in winning decks
text: Winning BR decks run about 9 Lizards cards among their 23 spells. The second tribe is usually Otters or Raccoons.

key: Card advantage whenever the opponent has lost life.
Counters on every creature once you have dealt damage.

archetypes.name: Expend ramp

text: Four-drops, mana sinks and the biggest bodies in the set. Every expend card triggers on the fourth mana, so the deck lives on its curve hitting four.

sections.heading: Tribes in winning decks
text: Winning RG decks run about 7 Raccoons cards among their 23 spells. The second tribe is usually Mice, then Squirrels.

key: A mana dork that grows with expend.
Ramps per raccoon and gains life on expend.

archetypes.name: Go-wide tokens

text: Go wide with tokens and offspring, then pump the team. The commons are strong in both colours, which makes it the most reliable deck to end up in. Second best by win rate.

sections.heading: Tribes in winning decks
text: Winning GW decks run about 9 Rabbits cards among their 23 spells. The second tribe is usually Mice, Frogs or Squirrels, about equally.

key: Grows with your board. One of the best uncommons.
Pumps every token and rabbit on each attack.

archetypes.name: Life-change flyers

text: Gain or lose life every turn to turn on the payoffs. Flyers, drain and the best removal in the format, though bats block poorly, so the deck wants to be the one attacking.

sections.heading: Tribes in winning decks
text: Winning WB decks run about 7 Bats cards among their 23 spells. The second tribe is usually Rabbits, then Lizards.

key: A flyer that taxes the opponent each turn you gain or lose life.

archetypes.name: Spells tempo

text: Spells-matter tempo on weak bodies. The weakest pair in the format. If you end up here, take interaction first and keep the creature count up.

sections.heading: Tribes in winning decks
text: Winning UR decks run about 7 Otters cards among their 23 spells. The second tribe is usually Rats, then Lizards.

key: Makes spells cheaper. Weak in practice.

archetypes.name: Forage midrange

text: Graveyard and Food midrange with forage payoffs. The guides disagree on how deep it is; the data rank it third. Black removal and green bodies carry it even when the forage cards don't show up.

text: Winning BG decks run about 8 Squirrels cards among their 23 spells. The second tribe is usually Raccoons, then Rats or Frogs.

Squirrel lord with menace that makes tokens.

archetypes.name: Valiant aggro

text: The fastest deck in the format. It needs creatures and spells that target your own creatures, so count your enablers before you count your payoffs.

key: Haste and valiant, but below average on its own.
Mouse lord that brings an equipment.

archetypes.name: Flicker value

text: Bounce or flicker your own creatures to reuse their enter triggers. Grindy and the best pair for a splash, since green has the fixing. Fifth by win rate.

text: Bloomburrow is a set about animal folk. There are ten creature types, one for each two-colour pair, and each comes with its own mechanic and game plan. It plays as a fast, creature-heavy format. Flyers matter, removal is scarce and most games are won on the board.

The numbers come from 17Lands Premier Draft data, checked against the Card Kingdom and Draftsim set guides. When a guide and the data disagree, the page goes with the data and says so. Where the guide says strong players, it means 17Lands users who win 60% or more of their games.

sections.heading: The format in short
list: Two colours, 16 lands, around 15 creatures. The Building a deck page has the numbers.
Card quality comes first. A deck of better cards beats a deck with a neater curve or creature count, and by a wide margin.

Synergy counts when a card really needs other cards and your deck has them. A build-around with enough support wins more than its cards would on their own, and one without support loses more. Sharing a theme is not enough: of the ten archetype themes, only UB threshold made decks win more. See Build-arounds.

Tribes still pull picks. Strong players like a creature of a type they already have, though less than a card in their colours, and they pass tribal payoffs when they have nothing to pay off yet. Winning decks are about half one tribe and half its neighbours (see Tribes).
White, black and green run deep. Blue has the weakest commons, none reaching 57, and red is the weakest colour overall.
BR, GW, BG and WB have the best deck win rates. UR and WU are at the bottom.
Rares swing games: 14 rares and mythics win at 62 or more, against 59.2 for the best common.
Each pair has a gold uncommon Mentor and a gold rare that show its plan (see each pair page). The Duos are commons with two creature types that bridge neighbouring tribes.

text: In the first five picks, take power and then removal. Bombs and Seasons come first whatever their colour, followed by black and white removal and the top uncommons. A strong gold signpost is a fine early pick; the BG and GW Mentors are both top-ten uncommons.

sections.heading: The first pick
text: Most of the time the first pick is simple: take the best card. Strong players do that a bit over half the time, and they take one of the top three almost always. The rest depends on how far ahead the best card is.

When it is only barely better than the next one, they take it about four times in ten. The cards are close enough that it comes down to which colour you like and which card keeps more decks open. A gold card ties you to two colours on pick one and a one-colour card to one, so when two cards are close the one-colour card is the safer start.
The bigger the gap, the less there is to think about. When the best card is clearly ahead they take it about seven times in ten. When it is far ahead, as a bomb usually is, they nearly always do.
Players who finished with seven wins and players who went 0-3 made this pick the same way. You can't win the draft on pick one, so don't agonise over it.

sections.heading: Bombs, and drafting around them
text: A bomb in your deck is a real edge, and two are a big one. It is easy to overrate, though. One bomb is one card in forty. Drawing it wins games, but so does a deck where every other card is slightly better, and the two are worth about the same. A bomb makes a good deck better. It won't rescue a bad one.

That is why strong players don't bend the draft around a bomb. They take it, they hope its colour comes, and if it doesn't they move on. They end up playing their first-pick bomb about four times in five, which is hardly more often than they play any other good first pick.

Some bombs are lords: they make one tribe better and want you to draft it. Go for it when the tribe is coming to you anyway. The Mouse lords show it best, since every extra Mouse in the deck makes them noticeably stronger. If the tribe dries up, keep the lord as a good card and fill the rest of the deck with the best cards in your colours.
Then there is splashing. A third colour for one card costs you consistency, so do it only for a real bomb and only with the fixing already in your pool. One gold rare has proved worth it:
cards: WG decks that splash it win far more of the games where they draw it.

sections.heading: Main colour and second colour
text: You don't draft two colours at once. Pack 1 gives you one colour: by the end of it you will usually have six or seven good cards in it and two or three in anything else. That's fine. The second colour gets decided in pack 2, mostly around picks 4 to 8, when the best cards are gone and you can see what the table is leaving alone.

A finished deck is about 13 cards of the main colour, 8 of the second and a couple of gold ones. The second colour is the smaller half, but its cards are just as good. This is where most drafts go wrong. The main colour fills up, picks keep going into it out of habit, and by pack 3 there are five playable cards in the second colour when the deck needs eight.

So count as you go. Once you have about seven good cards in your main colour, another average one doesn't add a card to your deck. It only pushes out your weakest. A decent card in the colour you are short of does add one. Say you hold seven black cards and two green, and the pack offers a black three-drop and a green three-drop that are about as good as each other: take the green one.
Expect waste. Around ten of your picks won't make the deck, even in a good draft.

sections.heading: Reading what is open
text: To read a draft you need to know who is passing to you. In packs 1 and 3 it is the player on one side. In pack 2 the direction flips and it is the player on the other side.

That matters because what you learn in pack 1 pays off in pack 3. If good green cards keep reaching you late in pack 1, the neighbour who passes to you isn't taking green, and the same neighbour passes to you again in pack 3. Pack 2 tells you about the other neighbour and is no guide to pack 3.

A signal is a good card that arrives later than it normally gets taken. A strong uncommon at pick 7 means six players passed it. Strong players drift toward the colour that keeps showing up like that, across all the packs they have seen.

Don't read much into the first few picks of a pack. A good card still there at pick 2, 3 or 4 is normal, because most good cards are still there that early. Strong players don't change course over it.
And don't assume only one colour is open. Often two colours flow freely while the other three are fought over. Finding one open colour tells you nothing about the others, so keep looking.

sections.heading: Tribes and synergy
text: Treat the tribes as a tiebreaker. If you already have three or four Rabbits, the next Rabbit is worth a little more to you than to anyone else. Strong players do take tribe mates more often, but a card in their colours still pulls harder than a card of their tribe, and by pack 2 the tribe counts for even less.

What they avoid is the payoff with nothing behind it. A card that rewards you for having Lizards is a poor pick when you have one Lizard, and it gets worse the later you take it, because there is less time to find the rest. The rare lords for rabbits, mice and rats are the exception and are worth starting a tribe for.

The other half of synergy is judging a card by the deck you are in. A win rate is an average over every deck that played the card. The same two-drop can be the weakest card in a white tribal deck and one of the best in a Food deck. The Build-arounds page lists the cards where the deck around them changes the most.

sections.heading: Spells and creatures
text: New drafters are often told to take creatures first. Strong players don't. When the best spell they can play is a little better than the best creature, they take the spell almost twice as often, and that stays true even when their pool is short of creatures. (About three times in ten they take a third card.) They take the better card and sort out the creature count later.

Cheap doesn't always mean early, either. Some cheap payoffs grow with your board and are really late-game cards. They cost little so that you can play two spells in a turn once the board is built. Don't count those as two-drops when you check your curve.

sections.heading: Where people go wrong
text: Splashy legends with poor win rates get taken early (see Traps). The Sleepers page lists cards that win more than their pick order suggests.

Winning and losing decks look almost the same: same creature count, same curve, same amount of removal, give or take a card. So the numbers above describe a normal deck and won't make one win. Card quality does most of that. The sections below cover the smaller things that still help.
Play two colours. Splash a bomb only, and only with real fixing; the set has very little.
Sixteen lands does a little better than seventeen, even though three in four decks run seventeen.

sections.heading: Lands
text: Most players run 17 lands out of habit. In this set 16 is better: decks with 16 win more, and that holds even for decks with a fairly high curve. The likely reason is that the format is fast and cheap, so a seventeenth land is more often a dead draw than a missing land drop. Don't go to 18.

For the split, count the mana symbols in each colour and then lean a little toward the lighter colour. Give it at least seven basics. In a 16-land deck that is two-thirds one colour, nine and seven is the normal split. Most players lean this way.
A land that taps for any colour does no harm in a two-colour deck. Cards that only fetch a basic are another story:
cards: Decks that run it do worse than their cards should.

sections.heading: Creatures and curve
text: Aim for 14 or 15 creatures. Decks with 12 or 13 win a little less and decks with 11 or fewer clearly less. Games here are won on the board.

The cheap end matters most. Have six or seven creatures that cost two or less; decks with three or fewer fall behind. Keep the whole curve low as well. The higher the average cost of your deck, the fewer games it wins.

sections.heading: Removal
text: You can't have too much removal, with one condition: it has to work by itself. Decks keep getting better with the fourth, fifth and sixth spell that simply deals with a creature.

Fight spells, bite spells and combat tricks are a different kind of card. They only work when you have a creature on the table, and usually a bigger one than theirs. On average, decks with four or five of them don't lose more. But they are the cards you sit holding when your board is empty and you are behind. So count them separately from your removal, and if a real removal spell and a trick are about equally good, play the removal.

sections.heading: Top end
text: Expensive cards are where decks get greedy. Three or four cards that cost five or more is plenty, and decks with two or fewer do just as well. A fifth costs you wins and a sixth costs more, since each one is a card you can't cast in the first four turns.

The ones worth the slots are the really strong ones. Two top finishers make a deck better than its cards suggest. Think of the rest of the deck as the part that keeps you alive and gets you to them, and cut the merely fine five-drops first.

sections.heading: Synergy
text: If you play a build-around, play it properly. With enough of the cards it wants, it makes the deck better, and a second one makes it better again. Without them it makes the deck worse, and by more than the support would have gained you. Find the support or leave the card in the sideboard.

Two things people expect to help don't. Plain card draw and mana sinks are worth their own win rate and no more: decks with three or more card-advantage spells win slightly less than decks with one. The card draw that pays off is the kind that comes with a build-around.
Three copies of an ordinary card are fine. Decks that play them do no worse.
Every tribe sits in two colours, but rarely half and half. If you know which colour holds most of a tribe, you know what a deck can do with one colour of it and what the other colour has to add.
The counts below are creatures of that type in each colour.

sections.heading: Where each tribe lives
list: Rabbits (GW): 7 white, 4 green, 4 gold. The white ones are much better, so any white deck can run a Rabbit package. Green mostly brings the payoffs for tokens and wide boards.
Bats (WB): 5 black, 4 white, 3 gold. Close to even, black slightly better.
Birds (WU): 5 white, 5 blue, 3 gold, plus one strong rare each in black and red.
Mice (RW): 6 white, 6 red, 3 gold. The red ones are better.
Otters (UR): 5 blue, 5 red, 3 gold. Only the blue ones are good. The red and gold Otters are among the weakest tribe cards in the set.
Frogs (GU): 7 green, 6 blue, 6 gold. The gold Frogs are the best of them and the reason to be in the pair.
Squirrels (BG): 6 green, 5 black, 3 gold. Even, and the gold ones are strong.
Lizards (BR): 8 red, 5 black, 3 gold. More of them are red but the black ones are better.
Rats (UB): 6 blue, 5 black, 3 gold. Even.
Raccoons (RG): 6 green, 5 red, 3 gold. Green's are better.

sections.heading: How tribal a winning deck is
text: Less than you might think. In decks with five or more wins, the main tribe is usually 6 to 10 of the 23 spells, about half of all the tribe cards in the deck. The rest come from one or two neighbouring tribes, and each pair page names the usual ones. Nobody wins with twenty Rabbits. There aren't enough good ones, and the Duos, with two creature types each, exist to bridge tribes.
list: Most tribal: GU with about 10 Frogs, then GW with 9 Rabbits and BR with 9 Lizards.
In the middle: BG with 8 Squirrels and RW with 8 Mice.
Least tribal: WB, UB, UR and RG with about 7 of their tribe, and WU with 6 Birds.
Rabbits turn up as the second tribe in every other white pair, most of all in RW.

sections.heading: What the second colour brings
text: A count of members undersells the second colour. Its part of the tribe is often the payoffs: the cards that want tokens, a wide board or a full graveyard. Those turn a pile of creatures into a deck. Before deciding a tribe lives in one colour, read what the cards in the other colour do.

Most cards are as good as their win rate in any deck of their colours. A removal spell kills a creature whatever else you drafted. A few cards are different: they get better with every card of a certain kind in the deck around them. A Mouse lord with six Mice is a different card from a Mouse lord with one.

These are build-arounds, and they cut both ways. Decks that play one with enough support win more than their cards would suggest, and decks with two win more again. Decks that play one without support lose more than that. It is true for strong and weak players alike.
The list below has the cards where the effect is big enough to be sure of.

sections.heading: The cards
text: Biggest effect first. Each note says what the card does best alongside, and how many of those cards decks usually run with it.
cards: Artifacts, non-creature enchantments and Food makers. About five.
Gift cards. Two is normal and each one helps a lot.
Food and cards that fill the graveyard, for forage. About five.
Mice. About six, though it is strong without them.
Best in the WB lifegain deck, alongside Bats. About four.
Cards that fill the graveyard. About four.
Squirrels, Bats, Lizards and Rats. About ten between them.
Best in the BG Food deck, alongside Squirrels. About three.

sections.heading: Look like build-arounds, not proven
text: These read like build-arounds. The results lean that way for some of them, but not clearly enough to count on. Pick them for their own win rate.
cards: Leans toward decks with Food makers. Just short of making the list.
Leans toward its four tribes. A bomb either way.
Token makers in the deck made no difference.
More Rabbits made no difference, though decks with two or three copies do well.

sections.heading: How to use this
list: Take a build-around when you already hold some of what it wants, or early enough to find it.
Once you have one, the cards it wants are worth more to you than their win rate says.
If the support hasn't come by the middle of pack 3, cut it. Playing one without support is the costliest mistake on this page.
A shared mechanic isn't support. Only count the kinds of card named above.

pages.title: Offspring
pages.summary: Pay extra to also get a 1/1 token copy
pages.verdict: Uneven. Good on cheap creatures with an enter trigger.

text: Pay the offspring cost on top of the mana cost and you also get a 1/1 token copy of the creature. It is best on cheap creatures whose enter trigger the copy repeats. On a plain body, the extra mana is rarely worth it. It shows up in every colour rather than one archetype.
cards: Offspring done right: a cheap enter trigger that the copy repeats.

pages.title: Valiant
pages.summary: Triggers the first time each turn you target the creature
pages.verdict: RW mice. Needs enablers that target your own creatures.

text: Valiant triggers the first time each turn you target the creature with a spell or ability you control. It is the RW mice mechanic, and it only works with enough pump spells, auras and creatures that target your own team.
cards: The best valiant payoff. Grows with every target and burns the opponent when it dies.

pages.title: Forage
pages.summary: Exile three cards from your graveyard or sacrifice a Food
pages.verdict: BG squirrels. One or two forage cards fit any deck.

text: To forage, exile three cards from your graveyard or sacrifice a Food. It is the BG squirrel mechanic, but one or two forage cards fit almost any deck, much like delve: the graveyard fills up on its own.
cards: Forage as a cost. Unconditional 2-mana removal once three cards are in the graveyard.

pages.title: Expend
pages.summary: Triggers when you spend your fourth mana in a turn
pages.verdict: RG raccoons. Four-drops and mana sinks make it work.

text: Expend triggers when you spend your fourth total mana in a turn. Every expend card in the set is expend 4, so the RG raccoon deck wants four-drops and mana sinks to hit it every turn.
cards: Expend payoff and mana dork in one.

pages.title: Gift
pages.summary: Your opponent gets a gift and your spell gets stronger

text: Gift cards let you promise your opponent something (a card, a Food, a tapped Fish, an extra turn of life) in exchange for a stronger effect. They create real decisions every game, and Draftsim calls gift the best gameplay mechanic in the set.
cards: Gift a Food to skip the life loss. Premium common removal.

pages.title: Threshold
pages.summary: A bonus once seven or more cards are in your graveyard
pages.verdict: UB rats. The one package with a clear deck-level effect.

text: Threshold cards get better once seven or more cards are in your graveyard. It is the UB rat mechanic: self-mill, surveil and loot to get there. Slow to switch on, strong once it does, and the only archetype package with a clear effect on deck win rate.
cards: Threshold turns an unblockable looter into pure card draw.

pages.title: Seasons
pages.summary: Mythic sorceries spending five pawprints across modes
pages.verdict: Four of the five are among the best cards in the set.

text: The five Seasons are mythic sorceries where you spend five pawprints across a list of modes. Four of them are among the best cards in the set. Red's is the exception, and people still take it early.
cards: Best card in the set by GIH. Edict, draw and drain modes.

pages.title: Food
pages.summary: Artifact token: {2}, tap, sacrifice: gain 3 life
pages.verdict: Fuel for forage and life triggers.

text: Food is an artifact token: pay {2}, tap and sacrifice it to gain 3 life. In this set it does more than gain life. It fuels forage, triggers the WB life payoffs and counts for a few other cards.
cards: Two bodies, two scrys and a Food.
Kills X/2s and leaves a Food behind.

pages.title: Class
pages.summary: Enchantments you level up with mana
pages.verdict: The green ones are premium; several others are traps.

text: Classes are enchantments that you level up by paying more mana over the game. The green ones are premium and a few others are traps, so judge each on its first level.
cards: Removal on entry that keeps paying off as you level it.

pages.title: Villages
pages.summary: Uncommon lands with creature-only coloured mana and a tribal ability
pages.verdict: Fine in their tribe, rarely a high pick.

text: The Villages are uncommon lands that make coloured mana only for creature spells and have a tribal ability. They are fine in their own tribe, but in a format where nearly every deck is two colours they are rarely worth a high pick.
The cards that take over a game. Most win through card advantage; one, the black mythic flyer, ends games almost on its own.
cards: Edicts, card draw and drain in one card. Take it over anything.
A rare reprint from the Special Guests bonus sheet. Every hit is a shock and a card.
Removal for three turns, plus two cards if you target your own creature.
A 2-mana lord for four tribes. Best in white tribal decks.
Card advantage engine for high-toughness creatures.
Mouse lord that brings its own equipment.
The true finisher. Opposing creatures drop to toughness 1 while it flies over with trample.
Makes an attacker or pumps the team on every attack.
Gives a mouse double strike every turn, and offspring doubles that.
Turns every other creature into Food and grows huge.
A +1/+1 counter every combat. Later it doubles counters.
A catch-up card that hands you life, tokens and mana.
A flyer that generates cards for every power-4 creature.
Removal, tokens and recursion in one card.
Counters, an artifact or enchantment wipe, and card draw.
Draw, copy and mass bounce. A reason to be in blue.

text: The Season to pass is red's. It wins at 53.6 and people still take it around pick 2 or 3.

Each real removal spell drawn is worth about 1.4 points of win rate over an average card from the same deck. Damage, fight, destroy and -X/-X spells all add about the same. Face burn, drain, counterspells, bounce and pingers add nothing measurable as removal. No type of removal beats another, and cheap removal does no better than the 4+ mana kind. Take real removal early. It runs out.
cards: An edict that hits their biggest creature.
Kills anything with power or toughness 4 or more.
4 damage to a tapped or attacking creature.
Fight for 1. The gift makes it safer.
Turns a creature into a Food. Close enough to removal.

cards: The worst uncommon in the set.

text: These rares get taken on looks. All of them go between picks 3 and 5 on average, earlier than an average common, and they win less often than one:
